title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in San Diego, CA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for San Diego welders, fitters and QC staff: shipyard and Navy work, California codes, Parts A, B and C. Study online or on site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in San Diego: A Six-Day Course for Shipyard, Construction and Manufacturing Inspectors
html:
San Diego builds and repairs ships, frames buildings in steel, and machines parts for aerospace and defense, and every one of those jobs ends with someone deciding whether a weld is good enough. In many contracts that person has to be an AWS Certified Welding Inspector. For San Diego welders, fitters, QC inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers who intend to sit the American Welding Society examination, Atlantis NDT runs a CWI preparation program that lasts six days, a 6-day course built around the three exam parts. You can work through it online with an instructor answering your questions, or a San Diego yard, shop or testing firm can host all six days on its premises for a crew of its own inspectors and welders.

Keep one fact in view: AWS, the American Welding Society, sets and grades the CWI examination and awards the credential to the people who pass it. Preparation is the whole of what Atlantis provides. It certifies nobody, never sees an examination paper, and holds no approval or endorsement from AWS. The full outline, exam structure and eligibility table are on the national AWS CWI exam prep course page; this page covers what is particular to San Diego.

San Diego's welding economy starts at the waterfront

The bay shapes the local market for welding inspection more than anything else. General Dynamics NASSCO runs a large shipyard on the San Diego waterfront, building and repairing vessels for the Navy and commercial owners. Naval Base San Diego is homeport to a large share of the Navy's Pacific surface fleet, and those ships go through scheduled maintenance periods that private repair contractors carry out under Navy oversight. Each availability involves steel replacement, piping repairs, foundation work and structural modifications, and each of those jobs generates welds that need inspection and records that need signing.

Shipyard work is not the whole story. San Diego County also has a steady flow of mid-rise and high-rise construction downtown and in the surrounding neighborhoods, laboratory and research buildings for the life-science sector, public works along the trolley and freeway network, and manufacturing that ranges from aerospace components to industrial equipment. Across the border, the Tijuana manufacturing base pulls fabricated assemblies and welded parts through the region's supply chain. Each sector has different codes, different customers and different reasons for wanting a CWI on the payroll.

The workforce pipeline reflects this. A 2024 report on the San Diego College of Continuing Education described a NASSCO fire-watch worker who heard about the college's welding classes from coworkers, completed the shielded metal arc welding certificate, and moved up to fitter. That path, from helper to fitter to welder to inspector, is common on this waterfront, and the CWI is often the step that turns production experience into a quality role.

Who hires certified welding inspectors in San Diego County

Employers that put CWIs to work locally fall into a handful of groups:

  • Shipbuilders and ship-repair contractors. Production quality departments need inspectors who can read drawings and specifications, check fit-up, verify preheat and interpass control, and accept or reject welds before compartments close up.
  • Structural steel fabricators and erectors. Shops supplying steel for buildings and bridges use CWIs for in-process and final inspection, and for the quality documentation customers and auditors review.
  • Special inspection and testing firms. On permitted building projects, firms retained by the owner send inspectors to verify structural welding for the building department.
  • Owner's representatives and construction managers. Public agencies and large private owners place inspectors on site to watch contractors, review welding procedure documents and keep records.
  • Manufacturers. Aerospace, defense and industrial equipment makers use inspectors at receiving, in the weld cell and at final inspection, and often need a certified person to satisfy a customer's quality requirements.

In practice, a San Diego CWI may move between these groups over a career. Someone who starts in a shipyard quality department may later work for a testing firm on construction projects, and the code book they study for Part C may change along the way.

Navy work, NAVSEA requirements and where a CWI fits

Naval ship work runs on Navy documents, not just on AWS codes. NAVSEA publishes fabrication, welding and inspection requirements for ship structure and for machinery, piping and pressure systems, and contractors working on Navy ships qualify their inspectors to those requirements under their own written programs. A CWI does not replace that Navy-specific qualification. What it does is give the inspector a nationally recognized credential and a solid foundation in welding processes, metallurgy, discontinuities and visual acceptance, which makes the Navy qualification easier to earn and the inspector more portable between yards.

That is why many waterfront inspectors carry both. If you work, or want to work, in ship repair, ask the quality department what inspector qualifications its program requires before you choose your path. For many people, the CWI is the credential they control personally, while the Navy qualification belongs to their current employer's program.

If you already inspect to Navy requirements, the CWI examination will feel familiar in places and foreign in others. The fundamentals and visual measurement skills carry over well. The code application part is different, because you will be answering questions from an AWS, API or ASME code book rather than from a Navy technical publication, and the structure of those books takes practice to navigate under time pressure.

Building, bridge and public works under California rules

Away from the waterfront, most CWI work in San Diego is driven by the California Building Code, which is based on the International Building Code. Structural welding on many permitted projects requires special inspection, and the building official decides which inspector qualifications are acceptable. For structural steel welding, the AWS CWI is the credential inspectors most commonly present, and the work itself is judged against AWS D1.1, the structural welding code for steel.

Bridge and transportation work adds another layer. Caltrans and local agencies use the AWS bridge welding code together with their own contract specifications, which can add or tighten requirements. An inspector on that work has to read the code and the special provisions side by side. If bridge fabrication is where you want to work, D1.5 may be the better code book for Part C; see the AWS D1.5 overview for how it differs from D1.1.

Earthquake design matters here too. Steel moment frames and braced frames in seismic regions carry demand-critical welds with notch-toughness and inspection requirements beyond ordinary structural work. Inspectors on those projects need to understand why certain welds get extra attention, and the metallurgy and testing topics in Part A of the exam lay the groundwork for that understanding.

Turning military and shipyard years into AWS eligibility

San Diego has a large population of veterans and active-duty sailors who weld for a living. Navy hull maintenance technicians, Marine Corps metal workers and Army allied trades specialists all build welding experience that may count toward the AWS requirement. AWS, not Atlantis, decides what qualifies. The rule of thumb is that experience must be welding-based work you can document and that someone can verify: production, repair, fabrication, inspection or design work on welded products.

The required years depend on education. With a high school diploma or equivalent, AWS asks for five years of welding-related experience; formal education in welding or engineering reduces that, and less schooling increases it. The full table is on the national course page. Before you study, gather what proves your history: service records, training certificates, performance evaluations that describe your duties, and contact details for supervisors who can confirm your work. Ask AWS how it wants military service documented before you submit the application.

Shipyard workers face a similar task. Fire watch and general helper time may not count the way fitting and welding time does, so list your roles with dates and duties rather than a single block of years. Being precise up front avoids an application that stalls in review.

Where San Diego candidates take the three exam parts

The examination has three parts. Part A covers fundamentals and Part C covers the code book you select; AWS delivers both as computer-based tests at Prometric centers, and Prometric operates test centers across Southern California. The hands-on Part B works another way: AWS stages it at selected seminar and examination venues, on dates AWS fixes, with specimens and gauges AWS hands you. San Diego candidates should check aws.org for the nearest Part B location and the available dates before planning study, because the practical date usually anchors everything else.

AWS asks for a minimum score of 72% on each part and sends one consolidated score report once all three are complete. Candidates also need to pass the AWS vision test, which covers near vision and color perception, before sitting the examination. For a closer look at where candidates tend to lose points by part, read the CWI results by exam part article. Exam charges are set by AWS and listed on aws.org; for a fuller budget that also counts a trip to the practical venue, work through the CWI exam budget planner.

Local training routes: SDCCE, Workshops for Warriors and the AWS San Diego Section

The CWI is not an entry-level credential, so most candidates arrive with years of welding behind them. Much of that experience in San Diego started in local programs:

  • San Diego College of Continuing Education (SDCCE). Its welding facility at the Educational Cultural Complex in the Mountain View neighborhood offers tuition-free certificates in shielded metal arc, gas metal and flux-cored arc, gas tungsten arc and pipe welding. The college has added robotic welding and plasma cutting equipment and received a workforce award from BlueForge Alliance to expand the lab.
  • Workshops for Warriors. This training school on Main Street hosts an AWS student chapter and has hosted meetings of the local AWS section.
  • Union apprenticeships and employer programs. Shipyards, fabricators and the building trades train welders on the job, and that documented time is what AWS will look at when you apply.

The AWS San Diego Section runs local meetings, including technical sessions where equipment makers have demonstrated new processes such as handheld laser welding. Section meetings are a practical place to meet working CWIs, ask about the Part B experience, and hear which employers are hiring. Details are on the section's page at sections.aws.org.

How the six-day course fits a San Diego schedule

Shipyard shifts, overtime during ship availabilities and construction schedules make it hard to take a week off. The course is built for that reality in two ways.

Individuals: online with instructor support

Preparing alone, you receive a study plan laid out along the six days, reading material, practice questions Atlantis wrote itself, timed mock papers, and a way to put questions to an instructor whenever a topic stalls you. There are no fixed class times. Many candidates spread the material over evenings and weekends, then use the timed papers in the final stretch before their practical date.

Employers: six days at your facility

A shipyard, fabricator or testing firm can bring the whole program onto its own site and run it for a crew of employees. On site, the practical preparation uses the employer's gauges and real weld samples from the shop floor, and the code practice can focus on the book the group will use at work. Each worker in the group files a personal application with AWS, and the experience and eyesight rules apply person by person; a company cannot vouch anyone past them.

The six days follow the national outline: two days of fundamentals (processes, terms, symbols, metallurgy, testing, discontinuities and safety), one day of practical measurement and visual acceptance, one day inside the code book, one day of timed practice exams, and a final day of weak-area review and exam logistics. All practice questions are written by Atlantis to the published body of knowledge; none comes from a real AWS examination.

Choosing a Part C code book in San Diego

AWS leaves the Part C book up to you. Pick it by asking which code sits on the desk at your current job, or at the job you are aiming for. Around San Diego the usual picks look like this:

Your work in San DiegoCode book to considerWhy
Structural steel for buildings, special inspectionAWS D1.1Building projects judge structural welds against it; see the AWS D1.1 overview
Steel bridges, transit structuresAWS D1.5Bridge owners specify it, often with agency provisions added
Aerospace and defense componentsAWS D17.1Aerospace fusion welding work is built around it
Process and power piping, pressure equipmentThe ASME choice: Section IX read alongside B31.1 and B31.3Plant and piping work qualifies procedures and welders under Section IX
Gas and liquid pipelinesAPI 1104Pipeline construction and utility work use it for welding and acceptance

Shipyard inspectors often pick D1.1 because its structure, acceptance criteria and qualification logic transfer well to ship structure, even though Navy work uses its own documents. Whatever you pick, study the edition AWS lists for the examination, which may trail the newest edition in print.

After the CWI: NDT and inspection paths in San Diego

A CWI judges welds mostly by visual examination and document review. When a job needs volumetric or surface testing, other qualifications come in. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, an employer certifies its own NDT technicians after training, experience and examination, and many San Diego CWIs add ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing to become more useful on the waterfront and on construction sites. Atlantis offers SNT-TC-1A-based training for that step; see NDT training in San Diego, VT Level 2 training and the method pages for ultrasonic testing in San Diego and magnetic particle testing in San Diego.

Other CWIs move toward Senior CWI, toward additional AWS code endorsements, or into supervisory quality roles at a yard or fabricator. Renewal matters on every path: AWS describes CWI certification on a nine-year cycle, with renewal applications at years three and six and recertification at year nine. Keep your vision record current and track the dates.

For more background, read CWI requirements and career impact, the weld inspection methods guide, and try rehearsing inspection steps in the Practical NDT welding workshop. The free NDT practice tests are useful if you are also working toward method certification.

Requesting a quote from San Diego

Tell us whether the course is for one person or a group, what each candidate's education and welding experience look like in outline, which code book each person intends to use for Part C, and whether anyone has already applied to AWS or picked a practical date. For on-site delivery, include the facility location, the gauges and weld samples you can provide, and the weeks that fit around production. Send it through the San Diego CWI exam prep enquiry; we reply within one business day.

Comparing other West Coast and Southwest markets? See CWI exam prep in Los Angeles, Phoenix and Seattle.

faq.q: Is there a CWI exam prep classroom in San Diego?
faq.a: No. Atlantis keeps offices in Houston and Hyderabad and nowhere else. San Diego candidates study online and send questions to an instructor, or their employer hosts the full six days on its premises. See the national course page for the outline.

faq.q: Does the six-day course make me a CWI?
faq.a: No. AWS sets the examination and grants the credential. Six days of preparation sharpen you for Parts A, B and C, but the AWS experience rules, its eye test, the application and all three exam parts remain yours to clear.

faq.q: Can my Navy welding experience count toward CWI eligibility?
faq.a: It may, if it was welding-based work you can document and someone can verify. AWS makes the decision. Gather service records, training certificates and supervisor contacts, and ask AWS how it wants military experience documented before you apply.

faq.q: Does a CWI qualify me to inspect on Navy ships?
faq.a: Not by itself. Navy ship work follows NAVSEA requirements, and contractors qualify their inspectors under their own programs. Many waterfront inspectors hold a CWI as their personal credential alongside the qualification their employer's Navy program requires.

faq.q: Where do San Diego candidates take the CWI exam?
faq.a: Fundamentals and code application go on a computer at a Prometric center in the region. The hands-on practical happens only where AWS stages a session, on dates AWS fixes, so look up the nearest venue on aws.org before you plan study time.

faq.q: Which code book should a San Diego shipyard inspector choose?
faq.a: Many choose AWS D1.1 because its structure and acceptance logic transfer well to ship structure. If you work on bridges, consider D1.5; on pipelines, API 1104; on aerospace parts, D17.1. Pick the code closest to the work you do.

faq.q: How much does the course cost?
faq.a: Course pricing is quoted for each request. Exam charges belong to AWS and appear on aws.org; the budget planner pulls the pieces together. Request a quote.

faq.q: Are the practice questions real AWS exam questions?
faq.a: No. Every practice question is original, written to the published body of knowledge. Atlantis has no access to the AWS examination or its question bank.

faq.q: Where can I meet working CWIs in San Diego?
faq.a: The AWS San Diego Section holds local meetings and technical sessions, and Workshops for Warriors hosts an AWS student chapter. Both are good places to ask about the practical and about local employers.

faq.q: What should I learn after the CWI?
faq.a: Many San Diego CWIs add NDT methods such as ultrasonic, magnetic particle or penetrant testing under an employer's SNT-TC-1A program. See NDT training in San Diego.
